subject: New to Bayes, brms, and have a few questions :)

messages.author: 73f393e023353e59
messages.subject: New to Bayes, brms, and have a few questions :)
parts:
Hi everyone,

Having just completed the "8 Step Program" outlined by Etz et al, 2017, I'm working on a multilevel ordinal response model with a mix of dichotomous, ordered categorical, and continuous predictors. The full model appears fine -- chains mixing well, Rhats = 1, large effective samples, pp_check() is a good fit, etc. -- but until now I've mainly just been messing around to get familiar with this (stellar!) package. I'd like to formally write-up these results and I've a few questions concerning best practices and model tweaks.

1) When multiple predictors are to be included, do you add each individually and sequentially, using WAIC or LOO methods to examine change in model fit? Or can you do them in batches? For example, include demographic variables, then add personality scores, etc. On a related note, if predictors don't add to the model do you drop them in subsequent rounds of model fitting, making note of the drop, or leave them in?

2) One of the papers I've looked at for inspiration (Kruschke & Vollmer 2014) used a similar response model but fixed the two extreme thresholds so all the threshold estimates were bound by the scale of the outcome variable. Is this possible in brms? Or even necessary or desirable? This point really has me confused. (I've compared flexible vs equidistant thresholds in brms and flexible affords the better fit by far. Additionally, the std error of each threshold estimate is small compared to the distance between successive thresholds, suggesting the model isn't having a hard time locating them in the latent space).

3) Do the advantages of centering predictors still apply when using brms? I've included centered predictors and noticed the marginal effects plots seem to "recover" the original scale of the predictor variables. I'm not sure what's going on here. (Note: I am using the scale() function on the fly in the brm model formula).

Any insight into the above would be greatly appreciated!

Cheers,

Ian

messages.author: 6e3dd74b422c061b
messages.subject: Re: [brms-users] New to Bayes, brms, and have a few questions :)
parts:
Hi Ian,

1) This is a very general question, with no general answer. Comparing models via LOO is a good idea but it really depends on your research question. For instance, if you are interested in a causal effect of a certain predictor, you would leave possible confounding variables in the model even if they don't improve model fit.

2) This isn't possible and I am not sure if it is desired. I would just go with the flexible thresholds. After all, they are just "intercepts" and ensure your models works correctly, but are rarely of interest themselves.

3) There is magic going on ;-) I don't like the scale() function really, since it triggers a lot of special behavior, which can be exploited (as brms does), but may also cause confusion in some sitatuations.
When modelling interactions, centering predictors around zero helps with interpretability of interaction coefficients, but it won't lead to an increase in sampling speed as brms already does not optimization in this regard internally.

Best,
Paul

parts:
Thanks, Paul.

After reflection, a reasonable answer to Q1 may be just to go with the convention in my field. Your clarification on Q2 is appreciated and I'll leave things as is, given no problems present. Concerning Q3, it sounds like using standardised factor scores would be a better way forward in this instance.

Kudos for such a great package; brms has truly opened new doors for me.

I.
